newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end up on jobless, inflation news.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end up on jobless, inflation news.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices halted a three-day losing streak on Thursday, ending sharply higher on news of more new jobless claims than expected and predominantly benign U.S. wholesale price figures.
The Labor Department said the U.S. Producer Price Index (PPI) rose 0.5 percent in December, a sharper rise than the 0.3 percent increase economists had anticipated.
But the core PPI, the index without its more volatile food and energy components, rose just a slight 0.1 percent.

The Labor Department also said that new claims for state unemployment insurance totaled 361,000 during the week ended January 4. It said claims in the previous week had totaled 374,000, revised up from the 366,000 originally reported.

"Today you had a Producer Price Index report where the overall rate looked bad, but the core rate showed no sign of inflation pressures either in terms of finished goods or intermediate (stage) goods," said William Dudley, chief U.S. economist and managing director at Goldman Sachs & Co.

"The market held in well, even with the stronger than expected PPI," said William Sullivan, senior vice president and fixed-income research director at Dean Witter Reynolds. "Part of that had to do with the subdued core PPI -- up just 0.1 percent," he said.
"And we interpreted the jobless claims data as indicating some deterioration in labor market activity and that's why we ignored the 0.5 percent PPI (rise)," Sullivan said.
Thursday's rally was also partly a preparation for a key economic report due on Friday -- the December employment data, traders and analysts said.
Spurred early by the jobless and inflation reports, the bond market climbed as the dollar rallied and stocks advanced.
Short-covering in the futures pit allowed March Treasury bond futures to end higher.
That same inclination to limit risk exposure to the December employment report let the 30-year bond extend its gain to more than a full point, traders said.
The benchmark 30-year bond finished at 96-25/32, up 1-4/32, to yield 6.75 percent on Thursday, versus Wednesday's closing yield of 6.84 percent.
"If the market had continued to go down, people would have been happy to stay with their short positions," one trader said. "But people ran for cover because the market went up."
Neal Soss, chief economist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp., said Thursday's rally was significant.

Market participation was lost because Christmas and New Year's Day each occurred in the middle of a week, Soss said. The Labor Department's scheduling of the monthly employment report release for the second Friday of the month, instead of the first, also delayed the start of the year for the financial markets, he said.
"So (for the financial markets), the year actually begins now and the market (on Thursday) said this is what we think the year will be about," said Soss.
"People believe that the economy is orderly, that the expansion continues with mild inflation, so they bought stocks. They bought bonds. They bought dollars," said Soss.

Two-year notes ended at 99-21/32, up 4/32, yielding 5.94 percent. Five-year notes rose 12/32 to 99-14/32, yielding 6.26 percent. Ten-year notes climbed 21/32 to end at 100 even, yielding 6.50 percent.
Three-month bill rates fell three basis points to 4.99 percent. Six-month bill rates slipped two basis points to 5.07 percent. Year bill rates ended five basis points lower at 5.26 percent.
-- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1660
